Applications such as healthcare, where the interpretability of AI models is essential for guaranteeing pa- tient safety and fostering confidence between medical professionals and AI systems, have seen the introduction of XAI-based procedures. Traditional deep learning models, though powerful in identifying tumors from MRI images, often operate as black boxes with limited explainability, making it difficult for clinicians to trust and validate their predictions. XAI techniques, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME, are integrated with CNNs to highlight the most relevant tumor regions and critical features in the images, providing visual and quantitative explanations for the model’s decisions. By focusing on abnormal brain tissues responsible for different tumor subtypes, XAI- enhanced models improve classification performance and generalizability, achieving accu- racy as high as 99% on known data and about 95% on unseen datasets. This combination of interpretability and accuracy helps clinicians better understand, trust, and adopt AI tools for diagnosis. Furthermore, XAI methods validate that the models do not rely on irrelevant features or overfit the data, making them robust and reliable for real-world clinical applica- tions. The use of XAI in this domain represents a significant advancement toward transpar- ent, accountable, and effective medical AI systems for brain tumor diagnosis and treatment support. XAI techniques such as feature importance methods, SHAP, LIME, rule extraction, and visualization approaches like activation maps–break down these complex models into understandable components. They reveal which input features have the most influence, explain individual predictions locally, and highlight the critical regions or factors contribut- ing to decisions. This transparency fosters trust, accountability, and facilitates identification of biases or errors that would otherwise go unnoticed in black-box systems. The computational overhead of XAI methods can be reduced through several strategies: ● Dimensionality reduction Applying data preprocessing techniques like principal com- ponent analysis (PCA) or feature selection to reduce the number of input features before explanation reduces the computational burden without significantly affecting interpret- ability. ● Sampling optimization Reducing the number of samples used in approximation tech- niques such as SHAP and LIME through intelligent methods like clustering-based or adaptive sampling balances accuracy and efficiency. ● Efficient surrogate models Using lightweight surrogate models (e.g., sparse linear mod- els or simplified decision trees) in place of complex approximations can lower compu- tational costs in post-hoc explanation methods like LIME. ● Hybrid methods Combining inherently interpretable models with XAI applied only when necessary helps limit overhead. For example, simple interpretable models can be used routinely, while complex methods like SHAP or LIME are reserved for high-risk cases requiring detailed explanations. ● Parallelization and hardware optimization Utilizing modern hardware such as GPUs or TPUs and parallel computing frameworks accelerates computation of feature attribu- tions in real-time applications. ● Lightweight and real-time models Designing and using XAI techniques specifically op- timized to run on resource-constrained devices or in real-time, such as backpropagation- based methods that require a single pass, can minimize overhead. JSON: Name: xai_guided_detector_classifier Title: An XAI-guided detector-classifier pipeline for MRI-based brain tumor localization and multi-class classification Short Hypothesis: Incorporating XAI-derived localization constraints into a detector-classifier training pipeline increases tumor localization IoU with expert segmentation masks by at least 5% while decreasing test-set multi-class classification accuracy by no more than 1% compared to an identical pipeline trained without XAI-derived constraints. Related Work: Prior work falls into three categories: (1) conventional machine-learning methods that use handcrafted texture/shape features with SVMs, RF, or KNN provide interpretable decision rules but lack sensitivity on complex MRI appearance; (2) deep CNN and transfer-learning approaches (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and transformer hybrids) deliver state-of-the-art classification and segmentation accuracy but operate as black boxes and often overfit to single-institution datasets; (3) post-hoc XAI approaches (Grad-CAM, CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME, SHAP, Layer-wise relevance propagation) have been applied to visualize model focus regions and produce feature attributions. Detection-first pipelines using object detectors (YOLO variants) combined with classifiers improve localization-to-classification workflows. Known limitations across these lines of work include: XAI explanations that are sensitive to noise and architecture, high computational cost for model-agnostic methods, lack of quantitative alignment between explanations and clinical segmentations, insufficient multi-institutional generalization, class imbalance handling, and a shortage of standardized evaluation protocols that jointly assess predictive performance and explanation fidelity. Abstract: This research develops and evaluates an XAI-guided detector-classifier pipeline for MRI brain tumor localization and multi-class classification. The proposed approach augments a two-stage workflow (fast object detection followed by a classifier) with a training-time XAI-derived localization constraint that encourages the model to align its internal attention with expert segmentation masks. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol that jointly optimizes classification accuracy and explanation fidelity, and a comparative study of multiple XAI algorithms (gradient-based and model-agnostic) used as supervisory signals. Expected outcomes are: measurable improvement in localization IoU against expert annotations, maintenance of classification performance within an acceptable margin, and quantitative metrics of explanation faithfulness and stability. The work enables rigorous evaluation of the trade-off between interpretability and predictive performance and produces practical evidence on which XAI methods yield clinically aligned explanations for MRI brain tumor detection and classification. Experiments: Datasets: train/validation/test splits drawn from BraTS (2020 or 2021) plus external holdout sets (FeTS2022, TCIA/REMBRANDT, and a Kaggle brain-tumor MRI collection) with standardized preprocessing (resampling to 1mm isotropic where applicable, intensity normalization, skull-stripping if present). Use tumor segmentation masks for localization evaluation. Baselines: (A) detection-classification pipeline without XAI supervision: YOLOv5/detr-style detector + classifier backbones (ResNet50, DenseNet121, ViT-GRU); (B) end-to-end classifier-only models (ResNet50, DenseNet121, ViT-GRU, MobileNetV2). Proposed variants: add XAI-guided localization constraint during classifier fine-tuning using (1) Grad-CAM-based attention regularization, (2) SHAP-based feature-attribution regularization, and (3) LIME-based local surrogate alignment. Metrics: classification accuracy, precision, recall, F1, multiclass AUC; localization IoU and Dice between heatmap-derived regions and segmentation masks; explanation faithfulness (deletion/insertion AUC), explanation stability (heatmap IoU across input perturbations), inference latency (ms/image), and clinician agreement (Cohen's kappa) on a sampled subset. Experimental setup: fixed random seeds, 5 independent repeats per configuration, early stopping on validation loss, same training schedule and augmentations across comparisons. Cross-institutional generalization test: train on BraTS+Kaggle, test on TCIA/REMBRANDT. Ablation studies: (i) compare with vs without XAI-regularizer; (ii) compare XAI methods (Grad-CAM vs SHAP vs LIME) as supervisory signals; (iii) detector-first vs classifier-only architectures; (iv) sensitivity to amount of segmentation supervision (100%, 50%, 10% mask availability). Statistical analysis: report mean±std over runs and use paired t-tests (alpha=0.05) to test hypothesis. Risk Factors and Limitations: XAI methods may be unstable: small input perturbations can produce inconsistent explanations, reducing reliability; model-agnostic methods (SHAP, LIME) incur high computational cost and may be impractical for real-time inference or large datasets; explanation alignment does not guarantee clinical correctness—heatmap overlap with segmentation masks may still miss clinically relevant features; dataset heterogeneity and scanner/protocol variation can limit generalization to other institutions; class imbalance and rarity of some tumor types can bias evaluation metrics and undermine minority-class performance; reliance on segmentation masks for XAI supervision assumes mask quality and availability, which may be limited; transformer-based or hybrid models can be prohibitively slow and require large compute resources for training and XAI computation; evaluation of clinician agreement is subjective and may require substantial expert time; regulatory, privacy, and data-sharing constraints may restrict access to sufficiently diverse multi-institutional datasets for robust validation.
